title: Visualizing the AI Education Debate
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky argues that the AI-in-education discourse has calcified into a repeating cycle of one-point solutions -- AI literacy, instructional redesign, detection, a return to analog classrooms -- that displace each other every few months without resolving anything, and that the popular "wicked problem" framework, while attractive, risks becoming an excuse for disagreement rather than a tool for understanding its structure. To break the cycle, he maps the debate into twelve distinct "modules" (access, authenticity, AI literacy, the teaching profession, governance, evidence, equity, data, curriculum, beneficiaries, cognitive/social development, and pace), showing how each one contains a self-reinforcing circuit of positions that generate pressure toward the alternatives they displaced -- for instance, banning AI access pushes students toward unsanctioned use elsewhere, which eventually pressures schools to reopen access. Rather than resolving any single module, Potkalitsky's real contribution is a set of structural observations that cut across all twelve: debates break open most productively when they generate a genuinely new question rather than adjudicating existing options, problems repeatedly migrate upward in scale from student behavior to institutional structure, and responsibility for systemic problems is routinely pushed downward onto teachers and students. He closes by concluding the exercise has not made the debate less wicked, but has made him less certain that wickedness requires staying trapped inside the same recurring arguments.
points: Potkalitsky diagnoses the AI-education discourse as a repeating cycle of one-point solutions (AI literacy, instructional redesign, detection, analog return) that displace each other every few months rather than accumulating into progress.

He identifies a risk within the popular "wicked problem" framework itself: treating a problem as inherently wicked can become a stopping point that excuses disagreement rather than a lens for understanding the debate's structure.

The twelve-module map (access, authenticity, literacy, teaching profession, governance, evidence, equity, data, curriculum, beneficiaries, development, pace) shows each sub-debate as a self-reinforcing circuit where each position generates pressure toward the alternatives it originally displaced.

A key structural pattern across modules is upward migration of scale: what begins as a question about student AI use repeatedly turns into a question about classroom design, institutional capacity, or the structure of schooling itself.

Potkalitsky observes that within hierarchical education systems, responsibility for structural problems is routinely pushed downward -- systemic issues become teacher problems, and instructional problems become student behaviors to monitor and correct.
quotes: On Substack and other social platforms, the discourse is dominated by one-point solutions. "Cultivate AI literacy." "Redesign instruction." "Track metacognition." "Grade process." "Detect student use of AI." "Return to the analog classroom." Every few months, the cycle repeats.

As attractive as the framework is, though, I worry about the way it may inadvertently keep us locked inside the rhetoric of thesis and antithesis. If we are truly grappling with wicked problems, why strive toward common solutions at all?

A ban limits sanctioned use in school while students continue to use AI elsewhere, which can eventually create pressure to reopen access. Open access without instructional redesign increases concerns about student offloading and produces pressure to restrict.

The problem repeatedly migrates upward in scale. What begins as a question about student use becomes a question about classroom design, institutional capacity, governance, or the structure of schooling itself.

Inside hierarchical systems of education, responsibility tends to be pushed downward. Systemic problems become teacher problems; instructional problems become student behaviors to monitor, regulate, or correct.

The work of visualization has not convinced me that the AI education debate is any less wicked than I thought. It has made me less certain, however, that wickedness requires us to remain trapped inside the same arguments.
